Every Broadway season seems to produce one show that confounds conventional wisdom. Incredibly, the quirky British musical Operation Men's Meat, now in its second year on the Great White Way, remains a massive hit. On paper, it sounds like an impossible cell. A tiny cast of five actors hold the stage for more than two and a half hours in a story based on an obscure World War II intelligence operation featuring a completely original score and no marquee names. Yet somehow against all theatrical odds, this scrappy import has become one of Broadway's most irresistible success stories. Inspired by the astonishing true story of the British deception campaign that helped pave the way for the Allied invasion of Sicily. It's infectiously clever, mixing farce, satire, history, and sentiment. Every theatrical device achieves maximum comic effect as the quintet of actors instantly transform into dozens of roles written by the comedy troop spit lip. The jokes often arrive in layers, piling on the laughs by the second and punctuated by musical numbers as inventive as they are hilarious and surprisingly moving. Beneath the show's manic comic energy lies genuine emotional investment as the versatile ensemble aly shifts from broad satire to genuine poignency. The show never loses sight of the real human stakes within the comedy. It's a difficult balancing act that few productions manage so gracefully. It may be Broadway's most ingenious bait and switch, a World War II caper about overlooked heroes who make history that's also a deeply moving musical for people who think they don't like musicals. At a time when Broadway increasingly relies on celebrity casting, cinematic adaptations, and recognizable cataloges, Operation Men's Meat has become a hit by trusting audiences to embrace originality. Sometimes the safest bet isn't the one with the biggest name in the deepest pockets. Sometimes all it takes is a brilliant idea, fearless execution, and a company of extraordinary performers to pull off the seemingly impossible. Operation Mincemeat has completed its mission, and Broadway is the richer for it. Woo!
